extracted.intended_audience: policy-makers, IP lawyers, patent office officials, and stakeholders involved in GCC and EU IP policy
extracted.subtask_short: GCC patents and designs law review
extracted.subtask_description: Comparative analysis of patent and industrial-design legal standards and procedures across GCC countries against international instruments (TRIPS, Paris Convention, WIPO treaties, EU practice), highlighting exclusions, terms, procedural requirements, and recommended reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusions from patentability — discoveries/scientific theories/mathematical methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Discoveries, scientific theories and mathematical methods shall not be regarded as inventions / shall not be patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed explicitly in multiple GCC laws (Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE). Presented as a basic excluded category consistent with international practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusions from patentability — computer programs and pure intellectual activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer programs, exercise of pure intellectual activities, or practice of a specific game are excluded from patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioned in Qatar, Kuwait and other GCC laws; often grouped with mathematical methods and pure mental acts as non-patentable subject-matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusions from patentability — schemes, rules and methods for doing business or performing mental acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Schemes, rules, and methods for doing business, performing purely mental acts or playing games shall not be regarded as inventions / shall not be patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appears across several national provisions (Kuwait, Oman, Saudi Arabia, UAE). Guidance implies exclusion of abstract or non-technical business/mental methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusions from patentability — plant varieties, animal species and biological processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Plant varieties, animal species, and essentially biological processes for the production of plants or animals (other than microbiological processes) are excluded from patent protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Found in Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and UAE with an exception often carved out for microbiological processes and their products; some national laws vary in exact scope and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusions from patentability — methods of surgical, therapeutic and diagnostic treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods of surgical or therapeutic treatment of the human or animal body and methods of diagnosis applied to the human or animal body are not patentable (with exceptions for products used in such methods).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit in Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and UAE; laws commonly exclude such medical methods while permitting patenting of products used in them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusions from patentability — natural substances and isolation processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural substances are excluded from patent protection, but the provision shall not apply to the processes of isolating those natural substances from their original environment; uses and processes of isolation may be protected where they constitute an invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically noted in Omani law: natural substances excluded but processes of isolating and certain uses may be patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusions from patentability — known substances with newly discovered use
rubrics_metrics.description: Known substances for which a new use has been discovered may be excluded; however, the use itself may be patentable where it constitutes an invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oman distinguishes between the substance (excluded) and a new use (potentially patentable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusions on public order, morality and Islamic Shariah grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions the commercial exploitation of which is necessary to protect public order, morality, or that are contradicting the principles of Islamic Shariah shall not be regarded as inventions / shall not be patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited in Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, UAE and GCC regulations; also includes national security carve-outs and special procedures for inventions affecting national security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent term and extensions for administrative/marketing delays
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents in GCC countries are protected for 20 years from the date of filing; some countries (Bahrain: up to 4 years; Oman: up to 5 years) provide extensions to compensate for delays in granting patent approval or delays in marketing approval (pharmaceuticals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These extension provisions go beyond TRIPS requirements and may conflict with Article 27.1 (differentiation by field). The report notes the EU practice of SPCs and critiques their impact on access to medicines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of priority — 12-month priority period
rubrics_metrics.description: The GCC Laws allow for the right of priority within a period of twelve months from the filing of the first application, in line with the Paris Convention and TRIPS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Right of priority is available for applications filed in Paris Convention or TRIPS member countries and under the PCT.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of International Patent Classification (IPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: All GCC countries use the international classification referred to in Article 1 of the Strasbourg Agreement Concerning the International Patent Classification (1979).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Saudi Arabia is the only GCC member of the Strasbourg Agreement, but all use the classification system as required by international practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace period for payment of maintenance fees (Paris Convention Article 5bis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 5bis of the Paris Convention provides a period of grace of not less than six months for payment of fees for maintenance of industrial property rights; Bahrain and Oman respect the 6-month grace period while four other GCC countries apply a three-month period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The shorter three-month period is inconsistent with Paris Convention and TRIPS obligations; recommendation to amend national laws and GCC Unified Regulations to adopt six months.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal of burden of proof for process patents (TRIPS Article 34)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the subject-matter of a patent is a process for obtaining a product, judicial authorities shall have authority to order the defendant to prove that the process to obtain an identical product is different from the patented process under certain conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bahrain, Oman and Saudi Arabia provide for this reversal of burden of proof as required by TRIPS Article 34; other GCC countries are encouraged to include similar provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compulsory licensing — alignment with TRIPS non-discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Compulsory licensing provisions are included in GCC laws as a TRIPS flexibility; however, UAE and Qatar provide that importing the product is not a legitimate reason for not granting a compulsory license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TRIPS prohibits discrimination between imported and locally-produced products; Qatar and the UAE should amend laws to comply. Compulsory licenses are important tools for antitrust, national emergency, extreme urgency, or public non-commercial use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural routes after end of GCC unitary patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Following the end of the GCC unitary patent, applicants must either use the Paris Convention route (filing in each GCC member state within 12 months) or the PCT route (national phase in each state).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some national patent offices (e.g., Saudi and UAE) are operational with online filing and substantive examination; others may delegate to the GCC Patent Office for registration procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: National patent office operational capacity and examination approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Some national patent offices (Saudi Arabia) examine patent applications in-house by qualified examiners; others (UAE) outsource examination of patent applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational capacity differences affect how applicants will proceed and whether national offices can handle substantive examination or will rely on outsourced/GCC-wide services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of industrial designs — coverage and clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Industrial designs should be defined broadly to cover appearance of whole or part of a product resulting from features such as lines, contours, colours, shape, texture and/or materials (EU Directive 98/71/EC model).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most GCC countries provide a definition (Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Saudi Arabia, UAE) but definitions differ and can be improved to cover all categories of designs; Qatar lacked an operative definition until recent law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions of protection for industrial designs — novelty and individual character
rubrics_metrics.description: Designs must be new and have individual character (or be novel/distinctive) and usable in industry or handicraft; designs contrary to public order or morality shall not be registrable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Saudi law requires new and original (individual character); UAE protects designs meeting any of these conditions; other countries require novelty. Registrability tests, disclosure rules and implementing regulations vary between countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special protection for textile designs (TRIPS Article 25.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: TRIPS Article 25.2 obliges members to ensure requirements for securing protection for textile designs do not unreasonably impair opportunity to seek and obtain such protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GCC laws do not provide special protection for textile designs as required by TRIPS; this is a compliance gap to be addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction between industrial design law and copyright law
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislation should address the interaction between industrial designs law and copyright law to clarify overlap and protection regimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GCC laws generally do not address this interaction, leaving legal uncertainty over protection routes for designs that may be eligible for copyright.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term of protection for industrial designs
rubrics_metrics.description: TRIPS requires that the protection for designs shall amount to at least ten years; EU practice allows up to a maximum of 25 years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GCC design terms are in line with TRIPS (minimum 10 years) but are less than EU maximums; registration generally mandatory for protection in GCC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration requirement for design protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Registration is mandatory for protection and there is no unregistered design right under the GCC laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Qatar, prior to the new law, designs were protected only via cautionary notices which are not statutory rights; recommendation to ensure statutory enforceable rights post-registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapting design protection to the digital age and enforcement modernisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Design law should be updated to address digital transformation: clarity on subject-matter, scope of rights and limitations (e.g., private use and 3D printing), accessibility/affordability, interoperability of protection systems, harmonisation on repair and spare parts, and improved enforcement using technologies like AI and blockchain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations derive from the EU evaluation of design legislation; GCC laws should follow similar evaluation to remain fit for purpose in the digital environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to WIPO and other international IP treaties
rubrics_metrics.description: GCC countries should join/adhere to key WIPO-administered treaties and other international instruments (e.g., WCT, WPPT, Marrakesh VIP Treaty, Beijing Treaty, Madrid Agreement/Protocol, Hague Agreement, Patent Law Treaty) to align with high international standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Membership is uneven across GCC states; accession supports national strategies for innovation and helps modernize procedures (e.g., elimination of legalized documents, multiclass trademark filings, international classification adoption). Specific treaty adherence would address gaps identified in national laws and FTAs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of TRIPS flexibilities and compliance (non-discrimination and scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: GCC laws incorporate some TRIPS flexibilities (e.g., compulsory licensing) but must ensure full compliance with TRIPS obligations such as non-discrimination between imported and locally produced products and other substantive TRIPS requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qatar and UAE provisions restricting importation as a reason for compulsory licensing contradict TRIPS; recommendation to amend laws accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplementary protection / extensions for pharmaceuticals (SPCs) and TRIPS consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensions of patent protection for delays (similar to SPCs) are provided by some GCC laws (Bahrain limited to pharmaceuticals; Oman broader) but may contravene TRIPS Article 27.1 by differentiating patents based on field of technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report notes the negative impact of SPCs on access to medicines and recommends careful consideration of EU practices before adopting extensions that harm local industry or violate TRIPS.
